name: MATHVISTA
description: MATHVISTA is a benchmark designed to evaluate mathematical reasoning of foundation models in visual contexts. It consists of 6,141 examples derived from 28 existing multimodal datasets involving mathematics and 3 newly created datasets (IQTest, FunctionQA, and PaperQA). The benchmark covers seven mathematical reasoning types (algebraic, arithmetic, geometry, logical, numeric common sense, scientific, and statistical reasoning) and five primary tasks (figure question answering, geometry problem solving, math word problem, textbook question answering, and visual question answering) across diverse visual contexts.
creator: Pan Lu, Hritik Bansal, Tony Xia, Jiacheng Liu, Chunyuan Li, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Hao Cheng, Kai-Wei Chang, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao
publisher: UCLA, University of Washington, Microsoft Research
inLanguage: English (with 6.57% non-English questions including Chinese and Persian)
citeAs: Pan Lu et al., MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts, ICLR 2024.
rai:dataCollection: MATHVISTA was collected by aggregating 28 existing multimodal datasets (9 MathQA datasets and 19 VQA datasets) and creating 3 new datasets (IQTest, FunctionQA, PaperQA). For existing VQA datasets, heuristic rules were used to automatically select examples likely to involve mathematical reasoning, followed by manual expert annotation. Each source dataset was limited to up to 400 examples to ensure balanced representation. The three new datasets were manually annotated by graduate students in STEM fields.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Only 85.6% of examples have annotations due to heterogeneity of source datasets. Annotations were sourced from original data providers, resulting in some examples lacking annotations.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Data was collected from 28 existing multimodal datasets including MathQA datasets (Geometry3K, GeoQA+, GEOS, UniGeo, CLEVR-Math, IconQA, TabMWP, SciBench, TheoremQA) and VQA datasets (ChartQA, FigureQA, DVQA, MapQA, PlotQA, DocVQA, AI2D, ScienceQA, TQA, A-OKVQA, KVQA, ParsVQA-Caps, TextVQA, VizWiz, VQA2.0, PMC-VQA, VQA-RAD, Super-CLEVR, VQA-AS). Three new datasets were created: IQTest (228 examples from puzzle test figures on online learning platforms), FunctionQA (400 examples from functional plots), and PaperQA (107 examples from academic papers released in August 2023 on Huggingface).
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: PaperQA sourced from papers released in August 2023 on Huggingface. GPT-4V evaluation dates range from Oct 7, 2023 to Oct 15, 2023. Multimodal Bard evaluation dates range from Sep 8, 2023 to Sep 10, 2023.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For VQA datasets, heuristic rules were designed to automatically select examples likely to involve mathematical reasoning. Examples with numeric answers or those containing quantity words in the questions were selected. Each source dataset was limited to up to 400 examples. The dataset was divided into testmini (1,000 examples) and test (5,141 examples) subsets using a sampling strategy to ensure balanced representation.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Automatic filtration using heuristic rules yielded 4,949 VQA-format examples. Three expert annotators manually labeled these examples to determine if they involve mathematical reasoning. Majority voting was used to finalize selections. Each source dataset was limited to up to 400 examples. Metadata including question type, answer type, language, source, category, task, grade level, and visual context were annotated. Mathematical reasoning categories were automatically annotated and verified by expert annotators for 1,000 examples.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: For VQA dataset labeling, three expert annotators manually labeled examples to determine if they involve mathematical reasoning, using defined criteria and annotation tools. For the three new datasets (IQTest, FunctionQA, PaperQA), all questions were manually annotated by graduate students in STEM fields using a two-step process: independent annotation by three reviewers followed by discussion to resolve disagreements. For mathematical reasoning category labeling, expert annotators manually labeled 1,000 examples from seven candidates. Human performance baseline was established using Amazon Mechanical Turk with annotators required to have a high school diploma or higher.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Custom annotation GUI tools (shown in Figures 22, 23, 24 in the paper) for expert annotation; Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) for human performance baseline evaluation.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Inter-annotator agreement for VQA mathematical reasoning labeling was measured using Fleiss Kappa score of 0.775, indicating substantial consistency. For the three new datasets, inter-annotation consistency rate was 99.2% (only 6 out of 736 questions had disagreements, resolved through team discussion). For automatic mathematical reasoning category annotation, 94.1% of examples had exact same set of reasoning types between automatic and human annotations, and 98.79% of individual labels were identical.
rai:annotationsPerItem: 3 annotators per item for VQA mathematical reasoning labeling and new dataset annotation; 5 annotators per item for human performance baseline on testmini subset.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Expert annotators for new datasets: graduate students in STEM fields. Human performance baseline annotators (Amazon Mechanical Turk): required to have a high school diploma or higher, history of completing more than 5,000 HIT tasks, acceptance score higher than 0.99.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: GPT-4 used as answer extractor (achieving >99.5% accuracy on 200 examples); EasyOCR (JaidedAI, 2020) for OCR text detection; Multimodal Bard for image caption generation.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The answer labels for the test set will not be publicly released to prevent data contamination; an online evaluation platform will be maintained. The benchmark is part of an ongoing research process with commitment to maintaining datasets, refining potential data noise in response to community feedback, and evolving the leaderboard in response to new models.
rai:dataSocialImpact: MATHVISTA is designed to facilitate the development of AI agents capable of tackling mathematically intensive and visually rich real-world tasks, with applications in educational disciplines, logical queries about statistical data, theorem proving, and scientific discovery. The benchmark highlights significant gaps between current AI models and human performance, underscoring the need for improvements in general-purpose AI.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset's focus on mathematical reasoning within visual contexts spanning specific domains like science and college-level math may limit generalizability. The dataset coverage may have gaps in representation of certain types of mathematical problems and visuals. Annotations lack a unified format and structure due to heterogeneity of source datasets.
rai:dataLimitations: While MATHVISTA encompasses a broad spectrum of tasks and visual contexts, there may be gaps in representation of certain types of mathematical problems and visuals. The dataset's focus on specific domains necessitates a more labor-intensive collection process, raising concerns about scalability and generalizability to other domains. Only 85.6% of examples have annotations. Annotations lack unified format and structure. The benchmark focused exclusively on the most recent and prominent models at time of publication.
rai:dataUseCases: Testing and evaluation of mathematical reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) in visual contexts. The testmini subset (1,000 examples) is intended for model development validation or for those with limited computing resources. The test set (5,141 examples) is for standard evaluation. The benchmark supports fine-grained evaluation across mathematical reasoning types, visual context types, task categories, and grade levels.
